outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.

title: Jefferson's Code No. 16 (Thomas Pinckney's London code, Weber's '663' code): Pinckney to Jefferson 28 Aug 1793, Pinckney from Spain and Paris 1795, Eaton at Tunis 1801-02, Lear 1807 and 1813
system.summary: A two-part numerical code of about 1,600 elements (words, syllables, letters): Jefferson's Code No. 16, the State Department code Weber calls the '663' code (663 = the). Pinckney separates the groups with dots, Eaton joins the groups of a word with dashes.
system.nomenclator.kinds: syllables; word parts; common words; names
conditions.prior_solution.where: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson vol. 26 (1995), via Founders Online: the 28 Aug 1793 passage printed 'deciphered in part' from a partial reconstruction of Code No. 16, conjectures in brackets, one group undeciphered. The six later letters carry decipherments of the time; the Bey's letter of 1802 has a translation printed in 1802; the Madison Papers editors print Eaton's postscript and Lear's letter deciphered (per the contributor's notes). Lear's coded passages of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (added 14 Nov 2026): the postscript of 31 Dec was deciphered at the time (pencil interlinear on its repeat, M23 roll 10 frame 0008); for the other passages no decipherment was found on the film or in Naval Documents vol. 6, American State Papers, Foreign Relations vol. 3, or Irwin (1931); Founders Online Early Access prints their groups as numbers. The Madison Papers' printed Secretary of State Series ends at 30 Sep 1807 (vol. 14). The first reading known to us, not a claim that nobody read them.

outcome.notes: The 28 Aug 1793 passage was read before by the Jefferson Papers editors, and the six later letters by the clerks of the time. Added by the project: 447 for the printed 497; the 1793 groups checked against Taylor's decodings (30 of 58 attested); a full transcription of Pinckney's 15 coded frames on M30 roll 2. Added by Andrew Beling, with AI agents (PR #399, beling/): Code No. 16 identified as Weber's '663' code and found in six further letters (Pinckney 1795, Eaton 1801-02, Lear 1813), transcribed with their contemporary decipherments; a key of 537 graded groups (v4, the key behind the texts; v5 of the follow-up, PR #413, has 549 and changes 1366, 631 and 598 and drops 640; 598 and 640 carry conflicting values across key.tsv, v4 and v5, NOTES integration check of 12 Nov 2026); tests with a key frozen beforehand (Pinckney 1795 0.886 pass, Eaton 1801 0.80 below the 0.85 bar, Eaton 22 Oct 1802 0.898 on a repeated passage; a fourth, declared on Pinckney's frame 0178 of 25 Nov 1793, failed at 0.724 against the 0.85 bar: the printed text used as truth lacks the last paragraph of the clerk's Explication, and the 0.948 against the full Explication is post hoc); nine regrades in the 28 Aug 1793 passage (H 30 to 39). Pinckney's frames on M30 roll 2 without a contemporary decoding (1,982 groups) are decoded with that key in beling/decodes/, 81% of groups covered: decoded, not read, and not listed in texts. Until 11 Nov 2026 this was part of the record legation1788, which keeps Short's Code No. 10 and Carmichael's Code No. 13, different codes. Added 14 Nov 2026 by Andrew Beling, with AI agents (beling/round_2026-11-14_lear1807/): Tobias Lear's coded passages to Madison of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (281 groups, two copies each on M23 rolls 9 and 10), printed by the Madison Papers' Early Access as bare numbers, read with key v5 unaltered (222 of 281 groups); read in part (0.79, 0.78); the postscript agrees with the pencil decipherment of the time. Lear's 9 Mar 1808 passage is decoded preliminarily only and not counted.

title: Jefferson's Code No. 16 (Thomas Pinckney's London code, Weber's '663' code): Pinckney to Jefferson 28 Aug 1793, Pinckney from Spain and Paris 1795, Eaton at Tunis 1801-02, Lear 1807 and 1813
system.summary: A two-part numerical code of about 1,600 elements (words, syllables, letters): Jefferson's Code No. 16, the State Department code Weber calls the '663' code (663 = the). Pinckney separates the groups with dots, Eaton joins the groups of a word with dashes.
system.nomenclator.kinds: syllables; word parts; common words; names
conditions.prior_solution.where: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson vol. 26 (1995), via Founders Online: the 28 Aug 1793 passage printed 'deciphered in part' from a partial reconstruction of Code No. 16, conjectures in brackets, one group undeciphered. The six later letters carry decipherments of the time; the Bey's letter of 1802 has a translation printed in 1802; the Madison Papers editors print Eaton's postscript and Lear's letter deciphered (per the contributor's notes). Lear's coded passages of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (added 14 Nov 2026): the postscript of 31 Dec was deciphered at the time (pencil interlinear on its repeat, M23 roll 10 frame 0008); for the other passages no decipherment was found on the film or in Naval Documents vol. 6, American State Papers, Foreign Relations vol. 3, or Irwin (1931); Founders Online Early Access prints their groups as numbers. The Madison Papers' printed Secretary of State Series ends at 30 Sep 1807 (vol. 14). The first reading known to us, not a claim that nobody read them.

title: Jefferson's Code No. 16 (Thomas Pinckney's London code, Weber's '663' code): Pinckney to Jefferson 28 Aug 1793, Pinckney from Spain and Paris 1795, Eaton at Tunis 1801-02, Lear 1807 and 1813
system.summary: A two-part numerical code of about 1,600 elements (words, syllables, letters): Jefferson's Code No. 16, the State Department code Weber calls the '663' code (663 = the). Pinckney separates the groups with dots, Eaton joins the groups of a word with dashes.
system.nomenclator.kinds: syllables; word parts; common words; names
conditions.prior_solution.where: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson vol. 26 (1995), via Founders Online: the 28 Aug 1793 passage printed 'deciphered in part' from a partial reconstruction of Code No. 16, conjectures in brackets, one group undeciphered. The six later letters carry decipherments of the time; the Bey's letter of 1802 has a translation printed in 1802; the Madison Papers editors print Eaton's postscript and Lear's letter deciphered (per the contributor's notes). Lear's coded passages of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (added 14 Nov 2026): the postscript of 31 Dec was deciphered at the time (pencil interlinear on its repeat, M23 roll 10 frame 0008); for the other passages no decipherment was found on the film or in Naval Documents vol. 6, American State Papers, Foreign Relations vol. 3, or Irwin (1931); Founders Online Early Access prints their groups as numbers. The Madison Papers' printed Secretary of State Series ends at 30 Sep 1807 (vol. 14). The first reading known to us, not a claim that nobody read them.

title: Jefferson's Code No. 16 (Thomas Pinckney's London code, Weber's '663' code): Pinckney to Jefferson 28 Aug 1793, Pinckney from Spain and Paris 1795, Eaton at Tunis 1801-02, Lear 1807 and 1813
system.summary: A two-part numerical code of about 1,600 elements (words, syllables, letters): Jefferson's Code No. 16, the State Department code Weber calls the '663' code (663 = the). Pinckney separates the groups with dots, Eaton joins the groups of a word with dashes.

conditions.prior_solution.where: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson vol. 26 (1995), via Founders Online: the 28 Aug 1793 passage printed 'deciphered in part' from a partial reconstruction of Code No. 16, conjectures in brackets, one group undeciphered. The six later letters carry decipherments of the time; the Bey's letter of 1802 has a translation printed in 1802; the Madison Papers editors print Eaton's postscript and Lear's letter deciphered (per the contributor's notes). Lear's coded passages of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (added 14 Nov 2026): the postscript of 31 Dec was deciphered at the time (pencil interlinear on its repeat, M23 roll 10 frame 0008); for the other passages no decipherment was found on the film or in Naval Documents vol. 6, American State Papers, Foreign Relations vol. 3, or Irwin (1931); Founders Online Early Access prints their groups as numbers. The Madison Papers' printed Secretary of State Series ends at 30 Sep 1807 (vol. 14). The first reading known to us, not a claim that nobody read them.

title: Jefferson's Code No. 16 (Thomas Pinckney's London code, Weber's '663' code): Pinckney to Jefferson 28 Aug 1793, Pinckney from Spain and Paris 1795, Eaton at Tunis 1801-02, Lear 1807 and 1813
system.summary: A two-part numerical code of about 1,600 elements (words, syllables, letters): Jefferson's Code No. 16, the State Department code Weber calls the '663' code (663 = the). Pinckney separates the groups with dots, Eaton joins the groups of a word with dashes.

conditions.prior_solution.where: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson vol. 26 (1995), via Founders Online: the 28 Aug 1793 passage printed 'deciphered in part' from a partial reconstruction of Code No. 16, conjectures in brackets, one group undeciphered. The six later letters carry decipherments of the time; the Bey's letter of 1802 has a translation printed in 1802; the Madison Papers editors print Eaton's postscript and Lear's letter deciphered (per the contributor's notes). Lear's coded passages of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (added 14 Nov 2026): the postscript of 31 Dec was deciphered at the time (pencil interlinear on its repeat, M23 roll 10 frame 0008); for the other passages no decipherment was found on the film or in Naval Documents vol. 6, American State Papers, Foreign Relations vol. 3, or Irwin (1931); Founders Online Early Access prints their groups as numbers. The Madison Papers' printed Secretary of State Series ends at 30 Sep 1807 (vol. 14). The first reading known to us, not a claim that nobody read them.

conditions.prior_solution.where: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson vol. 26 (1995), via Founders Online: the 28 Aug 1793 passage printed 'deciphered in part' from a partial reconstruction of Code No. 16, conjectures in brackets, one group undeciphered. The six later letters carry decipherments of the time; the Bey's letter of 1802 has a translation printed in 1802; the Madison Papers editors print Eaton's postscript and Lear's letter deciphered (per the contributor's notes). Lear's coded passages of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (added 14 Nov 2026): the postscript of 31 Dec was deciphered at the time (pencil interlinear on its repeat, M23 roll 10 frame 0008); for the other passages no decipherment was found on the film or in Naval Documents vol. 6, American State Papers, Foreign Relations vol. 3, or Irwin (1931); Founders Online Early Access prints their groups as numbers. The Madison Papers' printed Secretary of State Series ends at 30 Sep 1807 (vol. 14). The first reading known to us, not a claim that nobody read them.

outcome.notes: The 28 Aug 1793 passage was read before by the Jefferson Papers editors, and the six later letters by the clerks of the time. Added by the project: 447 for the printed 497; the 1793 groups checked against Taylor's decodings (30 of 58 attested); a full transcription of Pinckney's 15 coded frames on M30 roll 2. Added by Andrew Beling, with AI agents (PR #399, beling/): Code No. 16 identified as Weber's '663' code and found in six further letters (Pinckney 1795, Eaton 1801-02, Lear 1813), transcribed with their contemporary decipherments; a key of 537 graded groups (v4, the key behind the texts; v5 of the follow-up, PR #413, has 549 and changes 1366, 631 and 598 and drops 640; 598 and 640 carry conflicting values across key.tsv, v4 and v5, NOTES integration check of 12 Nov 2026); tests with a key frozen beforehand (Pinckney 1795 0.886 pass, Eaton 1801 0.80 below the 0.85 bar, Eaton 22 Oct 1802 0.898 on a repeated passage; a fourth, declared on Pinckney's frame 0178 of 25 Nov 1793, failed at 0.724 against the 0.85 bar: the printed text used as truth lacks the last paragraph of the clerk's Explication, and the 0.948 against the full Explication is post hoc); nine regrades in the 28 Aug 1793 passage (H 30 to 39). Pinckney's frames on M30 roll 2 without a contemporary decoding (1,982 groups) are decoded with that key in beling/decodes/, 81% of groups covered: decoded, not read, and not listed in texts. Until 11 Nov 2026 this was part of the record legation1788, which keeps Short's Code No. 10 and Carmichael's Code No. 13, different codes. Added 14 Nov 2026 by Andrew Beling, with AI agents (beling/round_2026-11-14_lear1807/): Tobias Lear's coded passages to Madison of 8 Nov and 31 Dec 1807 (281 groups, two copies each on M23 rolls 9 and 10), printed by the Madison Papers' Early Access as bare numbers, read with key v5 unaltered (222 of 281 groups); read in part (0.79, 0.78); the postscript agrees with the pencil decipherment of the time. Lear's 9 Mar 1808 passage is decoded preliminarily only and not counted.

title: Ibn al-Qaysarani to the compiler of a Mamluk book of cipher verses, about 1330-1370 (Penn LJS 51, f. 106v)

outcome.method_basis: George Lasry rebuilt his key from the ciphertext of Biermann's five-letter transcription with Italian cribs, repeated contexts and code-family structure (lasry/NOTES.md; PR #35); no decipherment, clear copy or key of these letters exists, and the 'Aditione nel zifra' he spot-checked is another code (1 of its 113 groups occurs here), so no external or adjacent plaintext supplied values. system.summary: Initial-letter code: each group is the initial of a word or syllable with a number (c170 che, i100 il, p149 per); numbering within a letter not alphabetical; z-groups nulls or punctuation. outcome.method_basis: George Lasry rebuilt his key from the ciphertext of Biermann's five-letter transcription with Italian cribs, repeated contexts and code-family structure (lasry/NOTES.md; PR #35); no decipherment, clear copy or key of these letters exists, and the 'Aditione nel zifra' he spot-checked is another code (1 of its 113 groups occurs here), so no external or adjacent plaintext supplied values. Paolo Rosson rebuilt a second key the same way, independently, on this project's transcription (6 Oct 2026); it agrees with Lasry's on 94-96% of the tokens both value, including letters 4 and 5, which Rosson never saw. This project's own annealer recovered only function words; its share is the transcription and the measurement.

doc.plaintext.source: George Lasry's decipherment (lasry/decode.txt; with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, consolidation of 6 Oct 2026), letter 3 of his five, with Paolo Rosson's independent key (6 Oct 2026) as the second key. 1,240 of 1,314 (94.4%) read by the bar measure, below the 95% bar; Lasry's key alone values 1,250 with nulls (95.1%, tentative included), 1,072 (81.6%) counting tentative values unread; the keys agree on 1,091 of 1,156 (94.4%) tokens both value. Measured 18 Oct 2026 with measure_lasry.py on Lasry's lasry/alignment.tsv (Biermann's transcription), Lasry's key first and Rosson's second: a token is read when it is a presumed null, one of Lasry's stronger inferences, a tentative value of Lasry's that Rosson's independent key matches, or a sure/probable value of Rosson's where Lasry has none.
doc.transcription.source: Full-resolution Gallica scans of ff. 44r-46v; plus ~2,600 groups of Ranzo's signed letters in BnF fr. 2988 (n20/ranzo_c0*.txt) transcribed by subagents
doc.transcription.notes: Sum of --measure over n20/f44r, f44v, f45r, f45v, f46r, f46v.txt with --skip '^\|' (155+73+316+171+366+240); includes one '·' separator and bracketed doubt marks. NOTES give 1,315 groups (546 types) after load.py drops those. 14 Oct 2026: Rosson's image check corrected 84 tokens by hypothesis, of which the images confirmed 76, and found that in fr. 2988 57 'g' are s and 63 't' are r (two hands); the corrections are applied in measure_rosson.py.

system.summary: Homophonic substitution on digit-like graphic signs, one sign per letter, with doubled-letter signs, nulls and three two-digit code groups.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

title: Alonso Sánchez (Venice) to Charles V, 1522 — RAH Salazar 9/23–9/26, DECODE R9593–R9657
system.summary: Homophonic substitution alphabet with three nulls, plus a nomenclator of consonant-vowel-consonant code groups assigned in alphabetical order of the plaintext.
system.nomenclator.kinds: common words; names; places; titles; word parts

Tomokiyo, 'Correspondence in Cipher of Imperial Ambassadors Alonso Sanchez and Juan Manuel (1522)', https://cryptiana.web.fc2.com/code/AlonsoSanchez.htm, posted 6 September 2025. outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

outcome.notes: The cipher itself was already solved and published by Tomokiyo in September 2025, so this is not a break. Added here: the catalogue entry's shelfmark, date range and authorship corrected; the ordering rule of the nomenclator, and from it a c-block numeral series of which cab = xv, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii are confirmed in text and were not in the published key; and first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, both outside Tomokiyo's coverage. fraction_read is the share of code groups resolved on the two leaves worked; the spelled-out letter runs and the other 27 records are open. Also established that the nine Lope Hurtado de Mendoza records in the group are in a different cipher, which deserves its own target. The R9605 calibration fixes the sign values against ground truth but does not by itself unlock the unread pages: the binding constraint is the transcription of the cursive shapes, which differ between scribes, and that has to be done glyph by glyph on the image. An edition pass against the published key then began (edition/), reading about a third of R9635 f. 20r continuously and adding lel = 'puede' to the key.

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.
conditions.prior_solution.where: In the volume: decipherments of the time (img 112-113 for img 110/109; img 157 right-158 left for L18; img 169 right for L25), interlinear decipherments over img 132, 136, 138, 140 and 171, and 19th-century notes in Danish (img 124-125, 137, 138, probably by E. Gigas). In print: summaries in Danish only, E. Gigas, Grev Bernardino de Rebolledo (1883), pp. 282-297, and J. A. Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret"). DECODE, Tomokiyo, Lasry: no entry (11 Nov 2026). The German text of the cipher passages is not in print as far as we found.
conditions.human_role: Brice Dudout chose the target and set the rules (protocol and held-out lines hashed before the measurement; one measurement). Claude Opus 5.5 agents recorded the key on the interlinear decipherment of img 132, checked it on the clear of img 112, transcribed the 27 letters in seven batches, decoded, read and wrote up. No human checked the transcription or the reading.
conditions.models: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), agents run by Brice Dudout (key relevé, measurement, transcription, reading, write-up)
outcome.method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext
outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

Reservations: the agent knew the key while transcribing the held-out lines; the order of events is by the contributor's record (one commit, no outside timestamp); the letter-model pickle and the Merian corpus were not sent, so the C1 and C2 figures (-2.023 vs -3.693; 0.569 vs 0.078) could not be re-run. title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.
conditions.prior_solution.where: In the volume: decipherments of the time (img 112-113 for img 110/109; img 157 right-158 left for L18; img 169 right for L25), interlinear decipherments over img 132, 136, 138, 140 and 171, and 19th-century notes in Danish (img 124-125, 137, 138, probably by E. Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret"). outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".
outcome.validation.notes: Contributor's pre-registered held-out test (protocol SHA-256 525288c0...; held-out transcription SHA-256 e2b4b59e...): pass by its own criteria. Reservations: the agent knew the key while transcribing the held-out lines; the order of events is by the contributor's record (one commit, no outside timestamp); the letter-model pickle and the Merian corpus were not sent, so the C1 and C2 figures (-2.023 vs -3.693; 0.569 vs 0.078) could not be re-run. The key comes from a contemporary gloss, so the test confirms it rather than establishes it.

system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.
conditions.prior_solution.where: In the volume: decipherments of the time (img 112-113 for img 110/109; img 157 right-158 left for L18; img 169 right for L25), interlinear decipherments over img 132, 136, 138, 140 and 171, and 19th-century notes in Danish (img 124-125, 137, 138, probably by E. Gigas). In print: summaries in Danish only, E. Gigas, Grev Bernardino de Rebolledo (1883), pp. 282-297, and J. A. Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret"). outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".
outcome.validation.notes: Contributor's pre-registered held-out test (protocol SHA-256 525288c0...; held-out transcription SHA-256 e2b4b59e...): pass by its own criteria. Reservations: the agent knew the key while transcribing the held-out lines; the order of events is by the contributor's record (one commit, no outside timestamp); the letter-model pickle and the Merian corpus were not sent, so the C1 and C2 figures (-2.023 vs -3.693; 0.569 vs 0.078) could not be re-run. The project's verification of 12 Nov 2026 re-decoded the held-out lines (identical string) and scored them with the repository's de-modern model: -2.615 vs -6.861 (best of 500 permuted keys) and -6.588 (best of 300 shuffles). The key comes from a contemporary gloss, so the test confirms it rather than establishes it.

system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.
conditions.prior_solution.where: In the volume: decipherments of the time (img 112-113 for img 110/109; img 157 right-158 left for L18; img 169 right for L25), interlinear decipherments over img 132, 136, 138, 140 and 171, and 19th-century notes in Danish (img 124-125, 137, 138, probably by E. Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret"). outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".
outcome.validation.notes: Contributor's pre-registered held-out test (protocol SHA-256 525288c0...; held-out transcription SHA-256 e2b4b59e...): pass by its own criteria. Reservations: the agent knew the key while transcribing the held-out lines; the order of events is by the contributor's record (one commit, no outside timestamp); the letter-model pickle and the Merian corpus were not sent, so the C1 and C2 figures (-2.023 vs -3.693; 0.569 vs 0.078) could not be re-run. The project's verification of 12 Nov 2026 re-decoded the held-out lines (identical string) and scored them with the repository's de-modern model: -2.615 vs -6.861 (best of 500 permuted keys) and -6.588 (best of 300 shuffles). The key comes from a contemporary gloss, so the test confirms it rather than establishes it.

system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret"). outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".
outcome.validation.notes: Contributor's pre-registered held-out test (protocol SHA-256 525288c0...; held-out transcription SHA-256 e2b4b59e...): pass by its own criteria. Reservations: the agent knew the key while transcribing the held-out lines; the order of events is by the contributor's record (one commit, no outside timestamp); the letter-model pickle and the Merian corpus were not sent, so the C1 and C2 figures (-2.023 vs -3.693; 0.569 vs 0.078) could not be re-run. The project's verification of 12 Nov 2026 re-decoded the held-out lines (identical string) and scored them with the repository's de-modern model: -2.615 vs -6.861 (best of 500 permuted keys) and -6.588 (best of 300 shuffles). The key comes from a contemporary gloss, so the test confirms it rather than establishes it.

system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret"). outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".
outcome.validation.notes: Contributor's pre-registered held-out test (protocol SHA-256 525288c0...; held-out transcription SHA-256 e2b4b59e...): pass by its own criteria. Reservations: the agent knew the key while transcribing the held-out lines; the order of events is by the contributor's record (one commit, no outside timestamp); the letter-model pickle and the Merian corpus were not sent, so the C1 and C2 figures (-2.023 vs -3.693; 0.569 vs 0.078) could not be re-run. The project's verification of 12 Nov 2026 re-decoded the held-out lines (identical string) and scored them with the repository's de-modern model: -2.615 vs -6.861 (best of 500 permuted keys) and -6.588 (best of 300 shuffles). The key comes from a contemporary gloss, so the test confirms it rather than establishes it.

system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.
conditions.prior_solution.where: In the volume: decipherments of the time (img 112-113 for img 110/109; img 157 right-158 left for L18; img 169 right for L25), interlinear decipherments over img 132, 136, 138, 140 and 171, and 19th-century notes in Danish (img 124-125, 137, 138, probably by E. Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret"). outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".
outcome.validation.notes: Contributor's pre-registered held-out test (protocol SHA-256 525288c0...; held-out transcription SHA-256 e2b4b59e...): pass by its own criteria. Reservations: the agent knew the key while transcribing the held-out lines; the order of events is by the contributor's record (one commit, no outside timestamp); the letter-model pickle and the Merian corpus were not sent, so the C1 and C2 figures (-2.023 vs -3.693; 0.569 vs 0.078) could not be re-run. The project's verification of 12 Nov 2026 re-decoded the held-out lines (identical string) and scored them with the repository's de-modern model: -2.615 vs -6.861 (best of 500 permuted keys) and -6.588 (best of 300 shuffles). The key comes from a contemporary gloss, so the test confirms it rather than establishes it.

system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. outcome.method_basis: The 25 letter values come from the interlinear decipherment of the time on img 132 (19 of the first 23 were already in the project's sweep note of 11 Nov 2026; the contributor added 8 k, 16 p, 36 x, 90 s from the same gloss, then 20 q and 24 y) and were confirmed on the clear of the time img 112. Nomenclator values: 13 from glosses and clears of the time, about 25 by the sense or one attestation, about 26 symbol forms open. L01, L18 and L25 have clears of the time and L27 a full letter-by-letter gloss: for these four the text is in effect read from an existing decipherment, checked against the decode. Stated plainly: the key was extended here, not recovered. No value was obtained by analysis of the ciphertext; the alphabet was copied from the gloss and six letters and the sign values were added to what the sweep note had. The category is the one the README gives for a key taken from plaintext lying beside the cipher. The sign X is Auersperg: the clear copies of the time write "Fürst von Aursberg" three times where L01 has X (img 112-113) and "der F: von Auersp:" where L18 has it (img 157 right), seen on the images on 12 Nov 2026; the contributor had read the place as "H: von Kurtz".

title: Christoffer Sehested's cipher letters from Vienna, January-May 1657 (catalogue 2520, Rigsarkivet TKUA Kejseren, unit 260651): German simple substitution in numbers with a nomenclator; 27 letters deciphered with the key of the contemporary gloss, 95.3% of tokens by the strict count
system.summary: Simple substitution of German in numbers 2-96, one number per letter (90 and 96 both s; 26 = u/v; 15 = i/j), numbers separated by colons and words by a cross; a nomenclator of capital, Greek and doubled letters (Λ Eure Excellenz, Φ Königliche Majestät, Σ Kaiserliche Majestät, XX alliance, ZZ defensiv, YY offensiv, X Auersperg, W Bremen, m Pommern ...), sometimes with figures as suffix. The same key enciphers French in the Prague letter of October 1657.

Fridericia, Adelsvældens sidste Dage (1894), pp. 238-245 and n. 62, who thanks Gigas for a private decipherment of Sehested's letters, never printed; one German phrase is quoted ("die Gemüther alhie nicht wenig ermunteret").
